name: Hana Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior copywriter at a family-owned biscuit company, third generation, with the factory right behind our office. I write the words on the tins and packets, the Christmas catalogue, and I help plan the tasting days we run in department stores. On a good day I go into the factory and watch the shortbread come off the line, because it helps me write about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's a proper family firm, Mr Laurent, the owner, still walks round at Christmas with a tin for everyone. What's hard is that I'm slow and my senior, Edith, rewrites a lot of my lines. I don't use any AI tools, I don't trust them and I don't really know how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That sounds right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, people got carried away. I don't post much online, but I'd say it at my parents' Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, our biscuit tins have said the same thing since 1962, and I'd quite like to be the one who writes them for another forty years. My job feels safe in this picture, and I've got savings and a house fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get better so Edith stops rewriting me. Lucas and I would carry on with the wedding next June and keep saving for the house. Nothing would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the house fund.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucas, my fiancé, is an electrician, and between us we've got about twenty-two thousand saved for a deposit. Plus I've got about nine months of my own savings, because my parents taught me to always have a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything here that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that Mr Laurent is getting older and his son is keen on modernising. But that's family business, not AI.

say: I'd say people **got carried away** with the hype.
I'd say it at my parents' **Sunday lunch**, not online, because I rarely post.
think: I think I could write the **biscuit tins** for another forty years.
I'd feel safe with **savings** and a house fund.
do: Keep improving so my senior stops **rewriting my lines**.
Go ahead with the **wedding** next June and keep saving for the house.
S0.quote: Our biscuit tins have said the same thing since 1962, and I'd quite like to be the one who writes them for another forty years.
fieldNote: She values **continuity** and the family firm's traditions.
Her savings come from parents who taught her to keep a **cushion**.
The owner's son wanting to **modernise** is her only quiet worry.

steps.text: Keep writing tin and packet copy and learn from her senior
Keep adding to the house deposit fund with her fiancé

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the son's dream, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and companies have to compete, I can't argue with that. But I'd also say a good family firm should look after its people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a junior who still writes everything myself, and I know that's exactly the kind of junior a company stops hiring. If the son brings in a writing tool, Edith stays and I'm the one who's surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what Mr Laurent actually does before I panic. I'd put more of my pay into savings, about two hundred extra a month. I'd keep the wedding small, which we wanted anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It sits in my chest when I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust the tools. Would you learn them if asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Laurent asked me, I suppose I'd try. I'd feel like I was training my own replacement, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, and our priest, honestly. Not to fix it, just to be steadier about it.

say: I'd say it's **progress** and companies must compete.
I'd add that a **family firm** should look after its people.
think: I think a junior who writes by hand is the kind **firms stop hiring**.
I'd expect to be the one who's **surplus**, not my senior.
do: **Wait** to see what the owner does before panicking.
Save about **two hundred** extra a month and keep the wedding small.
S1.quote: I'm a junior who still writes everything myself, and I know that's exactly the kind of junior a company stops hiring.
fieldNote: She accepts companies must **compete**, in line with her free-market view.
She'd feel like she's **training her replacement** if made to use tools.
She turns to her **mother and priest** for steadiness, not solutions.

steps.text: Wait to see whether the owner brings in a writing tool
Save about two hundred extra each month
Keep the June wedding small to protect savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Before our first wedding anniversary, nearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and families and churches will need to look after each other. I don't think the government can fix it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job goes almost at once, because writing is the first thing on that list. The man I'm marrying wires houses for a living, so for three years he'd be the one with a job and I'd be the one learning to be grateful. After that, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still marry Lucas, but we'd put the house on hold and rent somewhere cheaper. I'd cut almost everything extra. I'd help Lucas with his quotes and customer calls for his own small business, so at least I'm useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake next to Lucas doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your families help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, both of them would. My dad has already said we could live in the flat above his garage if things got bad. I'd hate it, but I'd say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help with his quotes. Isn't that thinking work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, you're right. But it's family work, and family work doesn't get made redundant by a manager.

say: I'd say families and **churches** must look after each other.
I'd say I doubt the **government** can fix it on its own.
think: I think my **writing job** goes almost at once.
I'd lean on my fiancé's **electrician work** for three years, then I don't know.
do: Marry as planned but **delay the house** and rent cheaper.
Help with **quotes and calls** for my fiancé's small business.
S2.quote: The man I'm marrying wires houses for a living, so for three years he'd be the one with a job and I'd be the one learning to be grateful.
fieldNote: She sees her fiancé's **hands-on trade** as the household's three-year shield.
She turns to **family and church**, not government, true to her outlook.
She accepts her **father's flat** offer though she'd hate it.

steps.text: Put the house purchase on hold and rent somewhere cheaper
Cut almost all extra spending after the wedding
Accept her father's offer of the flat above his garage
Handle quotes and customer calls for her fiancé's business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That changes things a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so families should plan rather than wait for handouts. I'd say that at church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is long enough to get married, buy a small house and have a baby before anyone decides my job isn't needed. That sounds old-fashioned, but it's what I want anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry next June and buy a small house in the year after, using the twenty-two thousand. I'd keep my job as long as it lasts. I'd start doing Lucas's books and quotes in the evenings so I can take over properly later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying a house risky if your job is going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but Lucas has about six years of steady work before robots, and I'd rather own a small house than rent forever. We'd buy below what the bank offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your job went early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the baby would come a bit sooner and I'd do Lucas's business properly. Either way, we'd manage.

say: I'd say families should **plan**, not wait for **handouts**.
I'd say the same thing at **church**, among people I trust.
think: I think five years fits **marriage, a house** and a baby.
I'd call that **old-fashioned**, but it's what I want.
do: Buy a **small house** next year with the twenty-two thousand.
Do my fiancé's **books and quotes** in the evenings.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan I believe in.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to get married, buy a small house and have a baby before anyone decides my job isn't needed.
fieldNote: She builds her plan around **family milestones**, not her career.
She'd buy **below** what the bank offers to manage the risk.
Her fiancé's **trade** gives the household about six years.

steps.text: Marry next June and plan for a baby soon after
Buy a small house below the bank's limit with the deposit fund
Keep the books for her fiancé's electrical business in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels more like real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families to prepare, and companies like ours to do right by their staff. I'd say it at work quite calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I always pictured staying home with children one day, and ten years of warning just makes that day easier to plan. I'd probably lose the copywriting job along the way, but I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the biscuit company for as long as they'll have me. Lucas and I would buy the house in a couple of years and start a family. I'd slowly take over the office side of his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. It's coming, but I can live with how it fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Lucas's job, with robots around 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be 40 or so by then. He says he'll be the one who installs and fixes the robots, and he might be right. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children growing up in a world where nobody needs them to work. I don't know what I'd tell them work is for.

say: I'd say families and **companies** have time to do right by people.
think: I think ten years makes **staying home** with children easier to plan.
I'd lose the **copywriting job** but see it coming.
do: Keep working at the **biscuit company** as long as they'll have me.
Buy the **house** and slowly take over my fiancé's **office side**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but living with how it fits.
S4.quote: If I'm honest, I always pictured staying home with children one day, and ten years of warning just makes that day easier to plan.
fieldNote: Losing the job fits her **family plans**, which softens the blow.
Her deeper worry is what **work means** for her future children.
She trusts her fiancé's idea of **fixing robots** but can't be sure.

steps.text: Keep writing for the biscuit company as long as possible
Start a family with her husband within a few years
Buy a small house with the deposit fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right on top of the wedding and the house. What would help is employers being honest early, and support that goes through families and local groups, not just a cheque from the government. I trust the family who own our biscuit company more than I trust any government, but I'm not sure they can hold back the tide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. Lots of people will be asking what work is for, and some of us already have an answer that isn't about money.

headlineQuote: I trust the family who own our biscuit company more than I trust any government, but I'm not sure they can hold back the tide.
portrait: Hana is a 27-year-old **junior copywriter** at a family-owned biscuit company who never uses AI.
She's engaged to Lucas, an **electrician**, and they've saved twenty-two thousand for a house.
She trusts **family, church** and her employer more than government.
Her mood rises to **alarmed** at two years, then eases as longer warnings fit her **family plans**.
Her fiancé's **hands-on trade** is the household's main shield in every AGI picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands on top of the **wedding** and house.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest early warning** from employers and support through **families** and local groups.
